## TL;DR

The Work board's search and quick filters were only half wired. The phone queue
keeps its search, priority, area, story and "Assigned to you" filters in the URL,
so they survive a reload. But at 720 px and up the desktop board ignored those
URL filters and gave no sign that tasks were hidden. The board now applies the
same filter predicate as the queue, shows the active filters in a chip bar at
every width, and offers a Clear filters control that removes only the queue
filter keys. Reload, project switch and clear-all are covered by jsdom tests
against fixtures (phone queue at 375 px, desktop board at 1280 px), and the
chip bar is rendered in headless WebKit at 375, 768 and 1280 px. Two gaps are
left for a human decision: sort and the human/held toggles are not namespaced
by project, and there is no search input at wide widths.

## Work and rationale

I read the task, then traced where search, filter and sort state actually live.
There is no search box on the desktop board. The search, quick filters and Reset
control live in `MobileWorkQueue.vue` and are written to the URL (#1138). The
desktop board keeps its own sort in the `repoos.board.sortOrder` localStorage key
and its human/held visibility toggles in two more global keys. The status filter
is a `?status=` query key.

The acceptance criteria asked for filters to be visible at 375, 768 and 1280 px.
At 375 px the queue shows its controls. At 768 and 1280 px (the narrow breakpoint
is 720 px) the board rendered and dropped the URL filters silently. That was the
concrete defect, so I fixed it rather than adding a new control.

Changes:

- `src/ui-app/src/lib/workQueueFilters.ts` is new. It holds the filter type, the
  reader from route query, the predicate, the active-filter check, the chip list,
  and a helper that removes only the queue keys. The predicate was moved out of
  the queue unchanged, so the queue and the board share one definition.
- `MobileWorkQueue.vue` now calls `matchesWorkQueueFilters` and imports the
  area-name helper. Its behavior is the same, and its existing tests pass.
- `BoardQueueFilters.vue` is new. It renders one chip per set filter inside the
  global `filter-bar` styles and emits `clear`. Its own style lets the chips wrap
  at 375 px.
- `WorkView.vue` applies the queue filters inside `visibleByStatus`, so the
  columns, the counts and keyboard navigation all see the same tasks. It renders
  the chip bar beside the status chip on the board view only. Clear calls
  `router.replace` with the query minus the queue keys, so `status`, `task` and
  `tab` are kept.

Tests (all passing, none skipped):

- `work-filter-persistence-qa-browser.test.ts` has 14 cases. Eight run jsdom
  behavior: board filters applied and shown, no chip bar without filters, reload
  with the same URL, clear-all scoped to queue keys, project switch landing
  unfiltered, and on the phone queue reload, Reset clearing all keys, and Reset
  disabled when inactive. Six WebKit cases render the chip bar with long and
  short filter sets at 375, 768 and 1280 px and assert nothing overflows the
  viewport.
- `work-queue-filters.test.ts` covers the pure helpers.

`docs/qa/2026-11-filter-persistence-qa.md` records the scope, the table of
results per width, the fixes, and the gaps.

## Approaches tried

I first considered adding a search input to the desktop board. It would have
introduced a new product control at wide widths, which the task did not ask
for, so I dropped it. The task asks for filters to be visible and clearable, and
the URL already carries them, so the smaller change was to apply and show them.

For the reload race where the URL watcher can overwrite a keystroke, I reasoned
that vue-router supersedes a pending `replace` with the later one, so the input
settles on the latest value. I did not change that code and did not add a test
for it, because I could not reproduce data loss in jsdom.

For per-project persistence I considered namespacing the localStorage keys by
`health.projectName`. The store reads sort at creation, before health loads, so
namespacing needs a second read after health arrives. That is a larger change
than this QA pass, so I documented it as a gap instead.

## Challenges and blockers

The WebKit suite needs the built stylesheet in `dist/ui/assets`, so it failed on
a clean worktree until I ran `bun run build:ui`. That is expected, and the suite
says so in its error.

The scoped check failed in `board-column-labels.test.ts`, in the DashboardView
block, which never touches my files. I bisected it. Dropping my `visibleByStatus`
change made it pass, and even a bare read of `route.query` inside that function
reproduced the failure. Skipping the WorkView block made it pass too. The cause
was three WorkView mounts in that file that were never unmounted. They stayed
live across tests, and once WorkView read the query during render they broke the
next DashboardView mount. The app unmounts WorkView on navigation, so this is a
test-isolation defect, not a production one. I added the missing `unmount()`
calls to those three tests, and the file passes 16 of 16.

The router mock in the existing tests is a plain object, not reactive, so the
board's `route.query` reads do not update after mount. That is fine for the
mount-per-case tests I wrote, but it means a test cannot change the query and
watch the board react. I did not need that case.

The desktop board has no way to set a queue filter, so visibility depends on a
URL. A human should decide whether the board needs a search control at wide
widths. This is a product question, not a blocker for this change.

No real device was used. The three widths are WebKit viewport emulations, so
touch targets and the native shell are not covered. Those need a human check.

## Key learnings

Search state that lives only in a narrow-screen component is invisible to the
rest of the app. The fix was to read the URL keys where the board renders, not to
duplicate the state. Moving the predicate into a shared module made the queue
and the board agree by construction, and the existing queue tests still pass.

A "per project" requirement needs a concrete definition before the code can meet
it. Here each project already has its own origin, so storage is separated in
practice. Only a same-origin switch would expose the global keys, and the UI has
no such switch. Writing that down as a gap is more honest than namespacing keys
on a guess.
